mainTopic: When can a person with a stake in a case, like a partner or a townsman, give up that stake and become a valid witness or judge?
overview: The גמרא asks how partners can testify for each other about their shared field, since each one seems to be a נוגע בעדות. It first says the witness wrote 'I have no claim on this field,' but a ברייתא shows that words alone do nothing. Next it says he gave up his share with a real קנין. Even then he still gains, because his creditor can collect from a field he once owned, as שמואל ruled about a seller. The גמרא answers that he took on אחריות only for losses caused by his own creditors, so he loses the same amount either way. It then asks whether giving up a share removes bias at all, citing ברייתות about a stolen ספר תורה and gifts to a city or its poor. It answers that a ספר תורה is different because everyone still benefits from hearing it read. It also says that a gift to poor people whom the town must support helps every resident. Finally, the גמרא returns to שמואל's statement that partners are שומרי שכר for each other.

steps.title: Why can partners testify? They are biased
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how partners can testify for each other about a jointly owned field, since each one has a personal stake.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why? They have a stake in their own testimony!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ruling just taught, that partners may testify for each other. It points out that a partner seems to be testifying for his own benefit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A witness who gains from his own testimony is a נוגע בעדות and is not accepted. A partner who testifies that the shared field belongs to his partner is really protecting his own share too. So how can the ruling allow it?

keyTerms.meaning: Why?
A witness who has a personal stake in his testimony, so his testimony is not accepted

phrases.english: Why?
phrases.notes: He is asking about the ruling right before this, that partners may testify for each other.

phrases.english: They have a stake in their testimony!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ruling that partners may testify for each other.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that partners may testify for one another.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A partner benefits from his own testimony about the shared field, so he should be a נוגע בעדות and be disqualified.

steps.title: The partner wrote that he has no claim on the field
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the case is where the testifying partner wrote 'I have no claim on this field,' so he no longer has a stake.
steps.simpleTranslation: What case are we dealing with here? Where he wrote to him: 'I have no legal claim or dealings with this field.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא narrows the ruling to a specific case. The witness had already written that he gives up any claim on the field.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the partner already gave up his rights in writing, then the outcome of the case seems not to affect him. So he is no longer biased and can testify.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here? (used to limit a ruling to a specific case)
'I have no claim or dealings' (a written statement giving up rights)

phrases.english: What case are we dealing with here?
Where he wrote to him:
phrases.notes: The partner who is testifying wrote this to the other partner.

phrases.aramaic: ״דִּין וּדְבָרִים אֵין לִי עַל שָׂדֶה זוֹ״.
phrases.english: 'I have no legal claim or dealings with this field.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge by limiting the case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Partners are always biased about their shared field.
steps.terutzMaskana: Here the witness wrote that he gives up all claims, so he is not biased.

steps.title: Just saying 'I have no claim' does nothing
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the answer by quoting a ברייתא: saying 'I have no claim on this field' has no legal effect.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if he wrote this, so what? Isn't it taught: One who says to his fellow, 'I have no claim on this field,' or 'I have no dealings with it,' or 'My hands are removed from it,' has said nothing!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the last answer. A ברייתא says these kinds of statements do not actually remove a person's ownership.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Words alone, without a proper act of acquisition, do not transfer or give up ownership. So the partner still owns his share and is still biased. The answer from step 2 fails.

keyTerms.meaning: And if so, what of it? (introduces a challenge)
But isn't it taught in a ברייתא?
My hands are removed (I give up my connection)
He has said nothing; it has no legal effect

phrases.english: And if he wrote this to him, what of it?
But isn't it taught: one who says to his fellow:

phrases.aramaic: ״דִּין וּדְבָרִים אֵין לִי עַל שָׂדֶה זו״;ֹ
phrases.english: 'I have no legal claim or dealings with this field';
or 'I have no business with it';
or 'My hands are removed from it' –
he has said nothing!
phrases.notes: Meaning these words don't take away his ownership at all.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי כְּתַב לוֹ מַאי הָוֵי? וְהָתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the answer of step 2 using a ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that writing 'I have no claim' removes the partner's stake.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא rules that such statements have no legal effect, so the partner still owns his share and is still biased.
steps.confusionAlert: This is not saying the partner lied. It says words alone are not a valid way to give up ownership.

steps.title: He gave up his share with a proper קנין
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the witness gave up his share through a formal act of acquisition (קנין), which does work.
steps.simpleTranslation: What case are we dealing with here? Where they made a קנין from him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a new case. Here the partner did not just say words but made a real קנין giving his share to his partner.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A קנין fixes the weakness from step 3. With a valid act of acquisition, his share really passes to his partner. Now the field is no longer his, so he seems unbiased.

keyTerms.meaning: They made a formal קנין with him, making the transfer legally binding

phrases.english: What case are we dealing with here?
Where they made a formal acquisition from him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a new answer to the original challenge after step 3 rejected the first one.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A written statement alone removes the stake (rejected in step 3).
steps.terutzMaskana: The partner transferred his share with a valid קנין, so he really no longer owns it.

steps.title: He still gains: his creditor can collect from the field
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges again: even after giving up his share, the witness still benefits, because keeping the field in place leaves it there for his creditor.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if they made a קנין, so what? He is keeping the field standing for his creditor!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the new answer. Even with a real transfer, the witness still has a hidden stake in the field.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The field was once his, so his creditor can still collect from it. If the field stays with his partner, the creditor collects from it and the debt is paid. If the field is lost, the creditor will come after the witness himself. So he is still biased.

keyTerms.meaning: He keeps it standing (preserves the field)
His creditor, someone he owes money to

phrases.english: And if they made a formal acquisition from him, what of it?
He is keeping it standing for his creditor –
phrases.notes: His creditor can collect from a field he once owned, so he wants the field to stay safe.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 4.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that a קנין removes the witness's stake.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Even after transferring the field, the witness gains when it stays in place, since his creditor can collect his debt from it.

steps.title: שמואל's rule: a seller cannot testify for his buyer
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא supports its challenge with שמואל's rule that a seller cannot testify about a field he sold, even without a guarantee, because he keeps it for his creditor.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רבין בר שמואל said in the name of שמואל: One who sells a field to his fellow without a guarantee cannot testify for him about it, because he keeps it standing for his creditor.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a source to back up the challenge from step 5. שמואל already ruled that this hidden benefit disqualifies a witness.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A seller who gave no אחריות owes the buyer nothing if the field is taken, so you would think he is unbiased. Still, שמואל disqualifies him because of his creditor. The same reasoning applies to the partner who gave up his share.

keyTerms.meaning: Without a guarantee; the seller does not promise to pay back if the field is taken
He may not testify

steps.whatToRemember: A person who once owned a field may still be a biased witness about it, because his creditor can collect from it. Both answers so far (a written statement, and a קנין) have been challenged. Step 7 gives the answer that saves the קנין case.
steps.whyThisMatters: שמואל's rule shows that being a נוגע בעדות is not only about owning something now. Any benefit, even an indirect one through a creditor, can disqualify a witness.

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר רָבִין בַּר שְׁמוּאֵל מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דִּשְׁמוּאֵל:
phrases.english: As Ravin bar Shmuel said in the name of Shmuel:
One who sells a field to his fellow
without a guarantee –
may not testify for him about it,
because he is keeping it standing for his creditor!

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּאָמַר רָבִין בַּר שְׁמוּאֵל מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דִּשְׁמוּאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Provides the source that supports the challenge in step 5.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that a former owner is biased because his creditor can collect from the field.
steps.raayaSupportSource: שמואל's ruling (via רבין בר שמואל) that a seller without אחריות cannot testify for the buyer about the field.

steps.title: The witness accepted financial responsibility
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the case is one where the witness took on אחריות, so keeping the field for his creditor gives him no gain.
steps.simpleTranslation: What case are we dealing with here? One where he accepted financial responsibility upon himself.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from שמואל's rule. It says the witness accepted אחריות for the field, so he is not biased.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The problem was that the witness wants the field to stay with his former partner so his own creditor can collect from it. If he took on responsibility, he will have to pay back his partner for whatever his creditor takes. So either way he loses the same amount and has no reason to lie.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here? (a formula that narrows the case)
He took upon himself
Financial responsibility or guarantee for a field, promising to pay if it is taken away

phrases.english: With what are we dealing here?
Where he accepted financial responsibility upon himself.
phrases.notes: "He" is the partner who is testifying, the one who gave up his share.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Steps 5-6 (he keeps the field for his creditor) by narrowing the case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The witness gains because his creditor can collect from the field if it stays with his former partner.
steps.terutzMaskana: He accepted אחריות, so whatever his creditor takes he must repay, and he has no gain.

steps.title: Responsibility for which losses?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what kind of אחריות is meant, and rules out general responsibility because that would make him even more biased.
steps.simpleTranslation: Responsibility for whom? If you say general responsibility, toward everyone, then all the more so it is good for him!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks which kind of responsibility the witness took on. It rejects the first possibility right away, and this sets up the real answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If he promised to repay his partner for any loss at all, then he badly wants the outside claimant to lose. If the claimant wins, the witness has to pay his partner. That would make him more biased, not less, so this cannot be the case.

keyTerms.meaning: If you say (introduces a possibility that will be tested)
General responsibility, covering a loss from anyone
All the more so
It is good for him, he prefers it

phrases.english: Responsibility for whom?
If we say general responsibility (toward everyone),
All the more so it is good for him!
phrases.notes: Good for him that the field stays with his partner, because otherwise he would have to pay him back.

steps.triggerLanguage: אַחְרָיוּת דְּמַאן? אִי נֵימָא אַחְרָיוּת דְּעָלְמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Clarifies the answer of Step 7 by asking what kind of אחריות is meant.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What kind of אחריות the witness accepted.

steps.title: Responsibility only for losses from his own creditors
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that the witness took on responsibility only for losses that come because of his own debts.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it means responsibility for a loss that comes to his partner because of him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the real meaning of the responsibility. He only promised to repay his partner if the field is taken because of his own debts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With this narrow guarantee, he does not care whether an outsider wins the field. If the field stays and his creditor takes it, he must repay his partner. If the field goes, he still owes his creditor. Either way he owes the same money, so he has no stake in his testimony.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather (introduces the accepted option after rejecting another)
Because of him, on his account

steps.whatToRemember: The witness is valid only if his guarantee covers losses from his own creditors and nothing more. Then he loses the same amount no matter how the case ends.

phrases.english: Rather, responsibility
For a loss that comes to him because of him.
phrases.notes: Meaning a loss to the partner that comes from the witness's own creditors collecting his debts.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 8 after rejecting general responsibility.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The אחריות covers only losses caused by the witness's own creditors.

steps.title: Does giving up one's share really remove bias? The stolen ספר תורה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא questions whether removing oneself from a share works at all, citing a ברייתא that a city's people cannot judge or testify about their stolen ספר תורה.
steps.simpleTranslation: And when he removes himself from it, is he really removed? But it was taught in a ברייתא: if the people of a city had their ספר תורה stolen, the case is not judged by that city's judges, and proof is not brought from that city's people. If it were so, let two of them remove themselves from it, and let them judge!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now goes back and attacks the earlier idea from Step 4, that a witness can give up his share and become valid. It brings a ברייתא that seems to show this does not work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Every resident owns part of the city's ספר תורה, so they are all biased. If giving up a share removed bias, the ברייתא should have said two residents can give up their shares and then judge or testify. Since it says no one from the city may serve, it seems that giving up a share does not help.

keyTerms.meaning: Removes himself, gives up his share or stake
But it was taught in a ברייתא (introduces a contradicting source)
Judges
And if it were so (if your claim were true)
Two people

phrases.aramaic: וְכִי מְסַלֵּק נַפְשֵׁיהּ מִינֵּיהּ – מִי מִסְתַּלַּק?
phrases.english: And when he removes himself from it, is he really removed?
phrases.notes: This goes back to Step 4, where the partner gave up his share with a קנין.

phrases.english: But isn't it taught in a ברייתא:

phrases.aramaic: בְּנֵי עִיר שֶׁנִּגְנַב סֵפֶר תּוֹרָה שֶׁלָּהֶן,
phrases.english: Residents of a city whose ספר תורה was stolen,
The case is not judged by the judges of that city,

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵין מְבִיאִין רְאָיָה מֵאַנְשֵׁי אוֹתָהּ הָעִיר.
phrases.english: And proof is not brought from the people of that city.
And if it is so,
Let two of them remove themselves, and let them judge!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי מְסַלֵּק נַפְשֵׁיהּ מִינֵּיהּ – מִי מִסְתַּלַּק? וְהָתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the אחריות discussion and attacks the basic idea from Step 4 that one can remove oneself from a share.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea in Step 4 that giving up one's share through a קנין removes bias.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא forbids all residents from judging or testifying about the stolen ספר תורה, and it does not suggest that two of them could give up their shares. This implies that giving up a share does not work.

steps.title: A ספר תורה is different because people hear from it
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that a ספר תורה is special because residents still benefit by hearing the Torah reading from it.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ספר תורה is different, because it stands to be listened to.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes away the proof from the ספר תורה. It says the ספר תורה case is special, so it tells us nothing about other cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even if a resident gives up his ownership share, he will still hear the Torah reading from that scroll in shul. So he keeps a real benefit and stays biased. Giving up a share can still work in normal cases, where no benefit is left.

keyTerms.meaning: It is different
It stands for listening, its purpose is to be heard from

phrases.english: A ספר תורה is different,
Because it stands to be listened to.
phrases.notes: Everyone hears the Torah reading from it, so even without owning a share they still benefit.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Deflects the proof of Step 10 by showing the ספר תורה case is unique.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ספר תורה ברייתא proves that giving up a share never removes bias.
steps.terutzMaskana: With a ספר תורה, a benefit (hearing the reading) remains even after giving up ownership. So the ברייתא does not show that giving up a share fails in general.

steps.title: Money left to 'the people of my city'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings another ברייתא: when someone leaves a מנה to his city's residents, no judges or witnesses from that city may be used. Why not let two give up their share?
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: one who says 'Give a מנה to the people of my city,' the case is not judged by that city's judges, and proof is not brought from that city's people. Why? Let two remove themselves and let them judge!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא to show again that giving up a share does not work. This time the case is money, where there is no 'hearing' benefit, so the last answer does not seem to fit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Money has no extra use like hearing a Torah reading. Once a resident gives up his share of the מנה, he should get nothing from it. Yet the ברייתא still says no one from the city may serve, which again suggests that giving up a share does not help. The next step answers this.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear (introduces a source brought as proof)
A מנה, a sum of one hundred dinars
Why?

steps.confusionAlert: This is the same challenge as Step 10, now with money instead of a ספר תורה. It is brought because the 'hearing' answer of Step 11 does not apply to money.

phrases.english: Come and hear:
One who says, "Give a מנה to the people of my city" –
The case is not judged by the judges of that city,

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵין מְבִיאִין רְאָיָה מֵאַנְשֵׁי אוֹתָהּ הָעִיר.
phrases.english: And proof is not brought from the people of that city.
Why?
Let two remove themselves, and let them judge!

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: הָאוֹמֵר ״תְּנוּ מָנֶה לִבְנֵי עִירִי״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Renews the challenge of Step 10 with a case the answer of Step 11 does not cover.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that giving up one's share removes bias (Step 4), as defended in Step 11.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Money has no leftover benefit like hearing the Torah reading. Yet the ברייתא still bars all residents and does not suggest that two could give up their shares. This implies that giving up a share does not work.

steps.title: The gift to the city is also for a Torah scroll
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers the question from step 12: the ברייתא about a מנה given to the city's residents is also talking about money for a ספר תורה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Here too, it is talking about a ספר תורה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from step 12. It says the gift of a מנה was for buying a ספר תורה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 11 the גמרא said a ספר תורה is special, because every resident benefits from hearing the reading from it. So giving up a share of ownership does not remove the bias. The same reasoning now covers the מנה case.

keyTerms.meaning: Here too: the same answer works for this case
A sum of one hundred זוז (silver coins)

phrases.english: Here too,
it is about a Torah scroll.
phrases.notes: He means the מנה was given so the town could buy a ספר תורה, like the case in step 10.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 12 using the answer given in step 11.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא seemed to describe a plain money gift, where giving up one's share should be enough.
steps.terutzMaskana: The money is for a ספר תורה, and residents keep benefiting from it even after giving up their share.

steps.title: A new source: a gift to the poor of the city
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא: if someone says 'give a מנה to the poor of my city,' the city's judges cannot judge and its people cannot testify.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: if someone says 'Give a מנה to the poor of my city,' we do not judge the case with that city's judges, and we do not bring testimony from that city's people.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a new challenge by quoting a ברייתא. The real question will come in a moment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This case seems to be about charity, not a ספר תורה. If giving up a share removes bias, why are all the townspeople ruled out? The גמרא will first fix the wording before asking this directly.

keyTerms.meaning: Come and hear: introduces a source used as a proof or challenge
The poor people of my city
Judges

phrases.english: Come and hear:
One who says, 'Give a hundred zuz to the poor of my city' —
we do not judge with the judges of that city,
and we do not bring proof
from the people of that city.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the ספר תורה answer, brings a case that seems to be plain charity money.
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea that a biased person can give up his share and become a valid witness.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Here the money is for the poor, not a ספר תורה, yet the whole city is ruled out.

steps.title: Why would the judges be ruled out if only the poor gain?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא questions the ברייתא's wording: the poor get the money, so why should the judges be unfit?
steps.simpleTranslation: And how can you understand this? The poor take the money, and the judges are ruled out?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out that the ברייתא, as written, makes no sense. The judges don't receive the money, so they should not be biased.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Only the poor gain from this gift. A judge who is not poor gains nothing, so there is no reason to disqualify him. This sets up a fix to the wording in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: And can you really think so? Signals the reading does not make sense
They take
They are disqualified

phrases.english: And can you really understand it so?
The poor take the money, and the judges are disqualified?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the wording of the ברייתא just quoted.
steps.kashyaTarget: The plain wording of the ברייתא.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: People who gain nothing from the gift have no reason to be biased.

steps.title: Fixing the wording: the poor judges and poor people
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rereads the ברייתא: only the poor judges and poor people of the city are ruled out.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, say: we do not judge with the poor judges of that city, and we do not bring proof from the poor people of that city.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא fixes the reading of the ברייתא. Only people who are themselves poor, and so would get some of the money, are ruled out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the bias makes sense: a poor judge or witness would get part of the מנה. This clears the way for the main challenge in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, say: introduces a corrected reading
Proof, here meaning testimony

phrases.english: Rather, say:

phrases.aramaic: אֵין דָּנִין בְּדַיָּינֵי עֲנִיֵּי אוֹתָהּ הָעִיר,
phrases.english: we do not judge with the poor judges of that city,
and we do not bring proof
from the poor of that city.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Fixes the problem raised in step 15.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: All the city's judges and people seemed to be ruled out.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only the poor ones, who would share in the money, are ruled out.

steps.title: Why can't two poor people give up their share?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: let two poor people give up their share and then serve as witnesses or judges.
steps.simpleTranslation: And why not? Let two of them remove themselves from the money, and let them judge!
steps.whatsHappening: Now comes the real challenge. If giving up a share works, two poor people could do that and become valid.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This repeats the challenge from steps 10 and 12 against the idea from step 4, that a person can remove his bias by giving up his stake. The ברייתא doesn't allow this, which suggests giving up a share does not work.

keyTerms.meaning: And why? Opens a challenge
Let them remove themselves (from their share)
Two people (the minimum for testimony)

phrases.english: And why not?
Let two of them remove themselves,
phrases.notes: He means give up their share of the מנה, so they gain nothing from the case.

phrases.english: and let them judge!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the corrected ברייתא to challenge the idea of giving up one's share.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that giving up one's share removes bias.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If it worked, the ברייתא would let two poor people give up their share and serve.

steps.title: This too is about a Torah scroll
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers again that the gift was for a ספר תורה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Here too, it is about a ספר תורה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the same answer as before: the money was meant to buy a ספר תורה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With a ספר תורה, everyone in town still benefits from hearing it read, so giving up a share does not help. That is why no one from the town can serve.

phrases.english: Here too, it is about a Torah scroll.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers step 17 with the same idea used in steps 11 and 13.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The gift seemed to be plain charity money.
steps.terutzMaskana: The gift is for a ספר תורה, so giving up a share does not remove the bias.

steps.title: Then why call them poor?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if this is about a ספר תורה, why does the ברייתא call the people 'poor'?
steps.simpleTranslation: And why does it call them 'poor'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא checks the answer against the wording. The ברייתא says 'the poor of my city,' which doesn't sound like a ספר תורה case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A ספר תורה belongs to the whole town, rich and poor. So the word 'poor' seems out of place.

keyTerms.meaning: It calls them

phrases.english: And why does it call them 'poor'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions how the answer in step 18 fits the word 'poor'.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How the word 'poor' fits a gift for a ספר תורה.

steps.title: Everyone is poor when it comes to a Torah scroll
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that compared to the cost of a ספר תורה, everyone counts as poor.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because everyone is poor when it comes to a ספר תורה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question about the word 'poor.' A ספר תורה is so expensive that every resident is 'poor' next to it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: So 'the poor of my city' simply means all the townspeople. This keeps the ספר תורה answer standing.

keyTerms.meaning: Next to, compared with

phrases.english: Because everyone, in relation to a Torah scroll —
are poor.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּהַכֹּל אֵצֶל סֵפֶר תּוֹרָה עֲנִיִּים הֵן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 19.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A ספר תורה is so costly that everyone is called poor in relation to it.

steps.title: Or: real poor people whom the town must support
steps.stepSummary: A second answer: the ברייתא means really poor people, whose support falls on all the residents.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say: really it is as it is taught, actually poor people, and poor people whose support is put upon the residents.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a different answer to step 17. The ברייתא is about real poor people, whom the townspeople are required to support.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the town must support these poor people, then a gift to them lowers what everyone else has to give. So every resident gains from the gift, not just the poor. Giving up a share of the money does not remove that gain.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you want, say: introduces a second answer
Really, actually
Who are placed upon them (whose support they must provide)

phrases.english: And if you want, say:
really it is as it is taught —
actually poor people,
and it is about poor people who are placed upon them.
phrases.notes: He means poor people the town has to support, so a gift to them saves everyone money.

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that bias can come from saving money, not only from receiving it.
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second answer to step 17, instead of the ספר תורה answer.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Second answer that reads the text plainly
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Only the poor seem to gain, so two of them could give up their share.
steps.terutzMaskana: Everyone gains, because the gift lowers what the town must give the poor.

steps.title: What case? If each person's amount is fixed, two can just pay it
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what case this is. If each person's charity amount is fixed, two people could pay their amount and then judge.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what is the case? If the amount is fixed for them, let two of them give what is fixed for them, and let them judge!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא checks the second answer by asking what the exact case is. It tests the first option and finds a problem with it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If each resident owes a set amount, two people could pay their full amount ahead of time. Then the gift saves them nothing, and they should be allowed to judge. So the second answer still needs to explain its case.

keyTerms.meaning: And what is the case? Asks for the exact situation
Where it is fixed for them (a set amount)
Let them give

phrases.english: And what is the case?
If the amount is fixed for them —
phrases.notes: He means each resident has a set amount of charity he must give.

phrases.english: let two of them give
what is fixed for them,
and let them judge!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests the second answer of step 21 by asking for the exact case.
steps.kashyaTarget: The second answer, that the poor are supported by the town.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the charity amount is fixed, two people can pay theirs and lose any bias, so they should be allowed to judge.

steps.title: The charity amounts were not fixed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא is talking about a place where each person's share of צדקה is not set.
steps.simpleTranslation: What case are we dealing with here? A case where the amount is not fixed for them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from Step 22. It explains that the ברייתא is talking about a town where nobody's charity share is fixed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 22 asked why two residents can't just pay their set amount, be free of any interest, and then judge. The answer is that no amount was ever set. Every resident could be asked to give more at any time, so all of them still have a personal interest in the case.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here? (a formula that narrows the case)
Fixed, set (an amount)

phrases.english: With what are we dealing here?
Where it is not fixed for them.
phrases.notes: "It" means each person's share of the charity for the poor. Since it isn't set, paying a share doesn't free anyone.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 22 by limiting the ברייתא to a case where amounts are not fixed.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought each resident could pay his fixed share and then judge with no personal interest.
steps.terutzMaskana: The shares are not fixed, so every resident always has a personal interest and cannot judge.

steps.title: Even with fixed amounts, everyone still gains
steps.stepSummary: A second answer: even if the shares are fixed, the residents still want the poor to get the gift, because more money for the poor eases everyone's burden.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or if you want, say: really, the amount is fixed for them. Still, they are pleased, because once there is a gain, there is a gain.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second answer. It accepts that the amounts are fixed but explains why the residents still have a stake.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This answer does not limit the case. Even with fixed shares, when the poor receive extra money, they will need less support from the town later. So every resident gains from the gift and still cannot judge.

keyTerms.meaning: If you wish, say (introduces another answer)
Really, actually (keeps the original assumption)
It is pleasing to them, they are happy with it
There is gain, relief

phrases.english: And if you wish, say:
Actually, it is where it is fixed for them,
and it is pleasing to them,
because once there is a gain, there is a gain.
phrases.notes: Once the poor have more, everyone in town feels the relief, since the poor will need less from them.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different answer to the same קשיא of Step 22, without limiting the case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rejecting the assumption that paying a fixed share removes all personal interest
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Once a resident pays his fixed share, he gains nothing more from the gift.
steps.terutzMaskana: Any gain for the poor lightens the whole town's burden, so every resident still benefits.
steps.whatToRemember: Two answers explain why residents cannot judge a case about a gift to their town's poor: either the shares are not fixed, or, even if they are, extra money for the poor eases everyone's load.

steps.title: Partners become paid guardians for each other
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא goes back to שמואל's statement about partners and quotes its next part: they become שומרי שכר for each other.
steps.simpleTranslation: And they become paid guardians for one another.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to שמואל's ruling about partners and quotes its second part. This sets up a new discussion of that line.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is not new text. The גמרא is quoting again from שמואל's earlier statement so it can now examine this specific part. The ruling says that partners are treated as paid guardians of the shared property for each other.

keyTerms.meaning: Paid guardians, who carry a higher level of responsibility for what they watch
For one another

phrases.english: And they become paid bailees for one another.
phrases.notes: "They" are the partners from שמואל's statement quoted earlier. The גמרא is picking up his words again.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the discussion of the town's poor and goes back to quote the next part of שמואל's statement about partners.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Partners are treated as שומרי שכר of their shared property for one another.
